name: Asymmetric Encryption
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Two Keys That Solve a Problem One Key Cannot
lesson.summary: Explains how asymmetric encryption uses a mathematically linked pair of keys, one shareable and one secret, to solve symmetric encryption's key distribution problem, and why it is usually paired with symmetric encryption rather than replacing it.
lesson.body:
Asymmetric encryption takes a fundamentally different approach from the symmetric model covered in the last chapter. Instead of one shared secret key used for both encrypting and decrypting, asymmetric encryption uses a mathematically linked pair of keys that perform different roles: one key encrypts, and only the other, different key in that pair can decrypt what the first one encrypted. Because the two keys in a pair are mathematically related but distinct, and because deriving one from the other is computationally infeasible even though they are linked, one key in the pair can be shared freely while the other stays secret.

This solves the key distribution problem from the previous chapter directly. If you want someone to send you a message securely, you do not need to exchange a shared secret with them beforehand over some other secure channel. You simply publish one of your two keys openly. Anyone can use that published key to encrypt a message intended for you, but because of the mathematical relationship between the pair, only the matching key, the one you kept secret, can decrypt it. Two strangers who have never met and share no prior secret can now establish secure communication, because the lock can be public even though the unlock stays private.

The mathematics behind this relies on what cryptographers call one-way functions, or more precisely, trapdoor functions: operations that are easy to compute in one direction but extremely difficult to reverse without a specific piece of extra information. RSA, one of the earliest and most widely deployed asymmetric algorithms, bases its security on the fact that multiplying two very large prime numbers together is computationally easy, while factoring that product back into its original two primes is, for sufficiently large numbers, prohibitively difficult with current computing methods. Other asymmetric systems, including the elliptic curve cryptography that most blockchain systems use, rely on different mathematical hard problems, but the underlying logic, easy forward, hard in reverse, is the same.

Asymmetric encryption is not simply a strict upgrade over symmetric encryption; it comes with its own tradeoff, which is speed. The mathematical operations involved are considerably more computationally expensive than symmetric encryption's operations, which makes asymmetric encryption impractical for encrypting large volumes of data directly. In practice, most secure systems use both: asymmetric encryption to securely exchange a temporary symmetric key over an insecure channel, and then fast symmetric encryption, using that now-shared key, for the bulk of the actual data.

Beyond solving key distribution, asymmetric key pairs turn out to have a second, equally important use that the next two chapters explore in detail: because only one key in the pair can produce something only its matching key can verify, the same mathematical structure can prove a message came from a specific party and has not been altered, which is the foundation of digital signatures and, ultimately, of how blockchain systems establish who is authorized to do what.
